questions.q: The apparent volume of distribution (AVd) is defined as the:
opts: Hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug in the patient's body, intravascular and extravascular
True plasma volume measured by dye dilution
Volume of blood cleared of drug per unit time
questions.exp: AVd is a hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug (intravascularly and extravascularly) in the patient's body - it is not a real anatomical space. (Book p9)

questions.q: A drug with a HIGH apparent volume of distribution is distributed mostly in the:
questions.exp: A drug with increased AVd is mostly in the extravascular compartment/tissue; one with a low AVd remains mostly intravascular/systemic. (Book p9)

questions.q: A drug that is largely confined to the intravascular compartment has:
opts: A low apparent volume of distribution
A high apparent volume of distribution
An AVd equal to total body water
An AVd independent of protein binding
questions.exp: Drug with low AVd - mostly in intravascular compartment/systemic; high AVd means extensive tissue distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: The formula for apparent volume of distribution is:
questions.exp: AVd = D(dose)/C0 x f, where C0 is the initial plasma concentration and f is bioavailability. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the AVd equation, C0 stands for:
questions.exp: C0 in the AVd formula is the initial plasma concentration measured after the dose; CT (used in the loading dose formula) is the target plasma concentration. (Book p9)

questions.q: For which route is bioavailability (f) equal to 1 while calculating AVd?
questions.exp: f = 1 for the intravenous route, since the whole dose enters the systemic circulation - so AVd = dose/C0 for IV dosing. (Book p9)

questions.q: The loading dose of a drug is calculated by the formula:
opts: D = AVd x CT x f
questions.exp: Loading dose D = AVd x CT / f, where CT is the target plasma concentration (a constant). (Book p9)

questions.q: In the loading dose formula, CT denotes:
questions.exp: CT is the target plasma concentration and is treated as a constant, so the dose varies directly with AVd and inversely with f. (Book p9)

questions.q: The relationship given for loading dose is:
opts: D is directly proportional to AVd/f
D is directly proportional to f/AVd
D is directly proportional to AVd x f
questions.exp: D is directly proportional to AVd/f, so a drug with a large AVd needs a larger loading dose to achieve the same target concentration. (Book p9)

questions.q: If the apparent volume of distribution of a drug increases, then to maintain the target plasma concentration:
questions.exp: Because D is proportional to AVd/f, if AVd increases the dose has to be increased to maintain the target concentration CT. (Book p9)

questions.q: How does obesity affect apparent volume of distribution?
opts: Increases vd only for water-soluble drugs
questions.exp: Fat content determines vd: obesity increases vd, while athletes (with less fat) have a decreased vd. (Book p9)

questions.q: Athletes have a decreased volume of distribution because they have:
questions.exp: Fat content is proportional to vd; athletes have a lower fat content and therefore a lower vd than an obese patient. (Book p9)

questions.q: Regarding sex differences in volume of distribution, the book states:
opts: Females, having a higher fat content, have a greater vd
Males have a greater vd because of higher muscle mass
vd is identical in both sexes
vd is lower in females due to lower albumin
questions.exp: Sex affects vd through fat content: F (females) with higher fat content > M (males). (Book p9)

questions.q: Plasma protein binding (albumin binding) relates to apparent volume of distribution as:
opts: Albumin binding is inversely proportional to vd
Albumin binding is directly proportional to vd
Albumin binding has no relation to vd
Albumin binding is proportional to vd squared
questions.exp: The book states albumin binding (plasma protein binding) is proportional to 1/vd - more binding keeps the drug intravascular and lowers vd. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the factors determining apparent volume of distribution?
questions.exp: The listed factors are fat content (obesity, athletes, sex), lipid solubility (pKa), albumin binding (inversely proportional) and tissue binding - renal clearance is not among them. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which property of a drug increases its apparent volume of distribution?
questions.exp: Lipid solubility (pKa) favours tissue distribution and increases vd, whereas albumin binding holds drug intravascularly and decreases vd. (Book p9)

questions.q: Digoxin is distributed to skeletal muscle more than to the heart because:
opts: Skeletal muscle has a greater mass
questions.exp: Digoxin distributes to skeletal muscle > heart due to the greater mass of skeletal muscle - although the heart is the target organ. (Book p9)

questions.q: The loading dose of digoxin is determined by:
opts: Lean body mass, not total body mass
questions.exp: Because digoxin distributes to skeletal muscle by mass, its loading dose is calculated on lean body mass and not on total body mass - a practical point in obese patients. (Book p9)

questions.q: When a drug has a very high volume of distribution, dialysis is ineffective because:
opts: Extravascular concentration is high and intravascular concentration is low
The drug is tightly bound to albumin
The drug is not filtered by the glomerulus
questions.exp: A very high vd means most drug is extravascular with little in plasma, so dialysis cannot remove significant drug - dialysis is ineffective. (Book p9)

questions.q: In toxicity due to a drug with a very high volume of distribution, treatment relies on:
questions.exp: Since dialysis is ineffective for drugs with a large vd, antidotes are given in toxicity. (Book p9)

questions.q: The mnemonic BADDOC is used for:
opts: Drugs with increased volume of distribution
Drugs bound to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein
questions.exp: BADDOC lists the drugs with increased vd - benzodiazepines, beta blockers, amphetamines, digoxin, opioids, organophosphates and calcium channel blockers. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which mnemonic groups drugs that are NOT cleared by dialysis?
questions.exp: BADDOC - benzodiazepines, beta blockers, amphetamines, digoxin, opioids, organophosphates, calcium channel blockers - are the drugs with a high vd, hence not cleared by dialysis. (Book p10)

questions.q: The specific antidote for benzodiazepine poisoning is:
questions.exp: The table pairs benzodiazepines (not cleared by dialysis) with the antidote flumazenil. (Book p10)

questions.q: Beta blocker overdose is treated with glucagon because glucagon:
questions.exp: The table pairs beta blockers (which block GPCR) with glucagon, whose antidotal action works by increasing cAMP. (Book p10)

questions.q: The antidote for amphetamine poisoning is:
questions.exp: Ammonium chloride is the antidote for amphetamines - it acidifies the urine and traps the basic drug for excretion. (Book p10)

questions.q: The antidote for digoxin toxicity is:
questions.exp: The book pairs digoxin (not cleared by dialysis) with the antidote Digibind (digoxin-specific antibody fragments). (Book p10)

questions.q: The antidote for opioid poisoning is:
questions.exp: The table pairs opioids with naloxone as the antidote. (Book p10)

questions.q: The antidote for organophosphate poisoning is:
questions.exp: In the table organophosphates are paired with atropine as the antidote. (Book p10)

questions.q: The antidote for calcium channel blocker poisoning is:
questions.exp: Calcium channel blockers are paired with calcium gluconate as the antidote. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which pair of poison and antidote is correctly matched as per the table?
questions.exp: Correct pairs are benzodiazepines-flumazenil, beta blockers-glucagon, amphetamines-ammonium chloride, digoxin-Digibind, opioids-naloxone, organophosphates-atropine and calcium channel blockers-calcium gluconate. (Book p10)

questions.q: Albumin binds predominantly to:
questions.exp: Albumin is the main plasma protein and binds acid drugs most commonly; basic drugs are bound by alpha-1 acid glycoprotein. (Book p10)

questions.q: Basic drugs are bound mainly to:
questions.exp: Alpha-1 acid glycoprotein is the plasma protein that binds basic drugs, whereas albumin binds acidic drugs. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which group of drugs is listed as bound to albumin?
questions.exp: Albumin-bound drugs listed are antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamide antibiotics, warfarin and aspirin. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which group of drugs is listed as bound to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein?
opts: Tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics (beta blockers, amiodarone, lidocaine)
questions.exp: Alpha-1 acid glycoprotein binds tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics - beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine. (Book p10)

questions.q: Warfarin and aspirin, both albumin bound, increase each other's plasma concentration when used together, leading to:
questions.exp: The book notes that albumin-bound drugs increase each other's plasma concentration if used together, and with warfarin plus aspirin this raises the risk of bleeding. (Book p10)

questions.q: When albumin falls, the sequence of events for a bound drug is:
opts: Decreased albumin - increased free drug - increased risk of toxicity
Decreased albumin - increased free drug - decreased effect
Increased albumin - increased free drug - increased toxicity
Decreased albumin - decreased free drug - decreased toxicity
questions.exp: Reduced albumin leaves more free (unbound) drug, and this raises the risk of toxicity - the classic example being phenytoin in nephrotic syndrome. (Book p10)

questions.q: When alpha-1 acid glycoprotein increases, the effect on drugs is:
opts: Decreased free drug and decreased effect
Increased free drug and increased effect
Decreased free drug but increased effect
questions.exp: An increase in alpha-1 glycoprotein binds more basic drug, so free drug falls and the effect falls. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which conditions are listed as causing a decreased albumin level?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, myocardial infarction
questions.exp: The clinical application box lists decreased albumin in nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus. (Book p10)

questions.q: An increase in alpha-1 acid glycoprotein occurs in:
opts: Inflammatory conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease) and myocardial infarction
questions.exp: Alpha-1 glycoprotein rises in inflammation - rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease - and after myocardial infarction. (Book p10)

questions.q: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome receiving a highly albumin-bound drug, you should expect:
opts: A greater free fraction of drug and an increased risk of toxicity
A lower free fraction and a reduced effect
No change in free drug because binding is unchanged
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome lowers albumin, so more unbound acidic drug circulates and toxicity risk rises - the book's 'decreased albumin - increased free drug - increased risk of toxicity' chain. (Book p10)

questions.q: In a patient with rheumatoid arthritis on a basic drug, a rise in alpha-1 acid glycoprotein will produce:
opts: A decreased free drug level and a decreased effect
An increased free drug level and an increased effect
Unchanged free drug because albumin compensates
questions.exp: Inflammatory states raise alpha-1 acid glycoprotein, which binds more basic drug, lowering free drug and reducing the effect. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which two plasma protein-patient condition pairs are correctly matched?
opts: Albumin - nephrotic syndrome (low); alpha-1 acid glycoprotein - myocardial infarction (high)
Albumin - rheumatoid arthritis (high); alpha-1 acid glycoprotein - cirrhosis (low)
Albumin - myocardial infarction (high); alpha-1 acid glycoprotein - CKD (low)
Albumin - diabetes mellitus (high); alpha-1 acid glycoprotein - nephrotic syndrome (high)
questions.exp: Albumin is reduced in nephrotic syndrome, CKD, cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus; alpha-1 acid glycoprotein is increased in inflammation and myocardial infarction. (Book p10)

units.title: Apparent Volume of Distribution: The Concept
units.guide: Apparent volume of distribution is the hypothetical volume of plasma in litres required to account for the total drug in the body, intravascular plus extravascular. A drug with a high AVd hides in tissue, while a drug with a low AVd stays in the systemic circulation.

units.title: Calculating AVd and Loading Dose
units.guide: AVd = dose/C0 x f, with C0 the initial plasma concentration and f the bioavailability (f = 1 for IV). The loading dose needed to hit a target concentration CT is D = AVd x CT/f, so D is proportional to AVd/f - when AVd rises, the dose must rise with it to keep the target concentration.

units.title: What Determines vd: Fat, pKa, Binding
units.guide: Body fat content drives vd upwards in obesity and downwards in athletes, and females with more fat have a higher vd than males. Lipid solubility (pKa) and tissue binding increase vd, whereas plasma albumin binding is inversely proportional to vd because it keeps the drug inside the vessels.

units.title: Digoxin: Muscle Mass and Lean Body Weight
units.guide: Digoxin distributes to skeletal muscle far more than to the heart because skeletal muscle has the greater mass, even though the heart is the target organ. Consequently the loading dose of digoxin is calculated on lean body mass and not on total body mass.

units.title: High vd: Why Dialysis Fails
units.guide: When vd is very high, the drug concentrates in tissue, so intravascular levels are low and removal methods like dialysis clear almost nothing; this makes dialysis ineffective. Toxicity of such drugs is therefore managed with specific antidotes.

units.title: BADDOC and the Antidote Table
units.guide: BADDOC - benzodiazepines, beta blockers, amphetamines, digoxin, opioids, organophosphates and calcium channel blockers - are the drugs with an increased vd that dialysis cannot clear, so each has an antidote: flumazenil, glucagon (which raises cAMP), ammonium chloride, Digibind, naloxone, atropine and calcium gluconate respectively.

units.title: Albumin and Alpha-1 Acid Glycoprotein
units.guide: Albumin, the commonest carrier, binds acidic drugs - antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, warfarin and aspirin - while alpha-1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs such as tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and the antiarrhythmics beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine. Two albumin-bound drugs used together, classically warfarin and aspirin, raise each other's plasma concentration and cause bleeding.

units.title: Hypoalbuminaemia, Inflammation and Drug Effect
units.guide: Falling albumin leaves more free drug and increases the risk of toxicity, and albumin is low in nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus. Conversely inflammation and myocardial infarction raise alpha-1 acid glycoprotein, which binds basic drugs more avidly, lowering free drug and the effect - the same disease state can therefore alter drug handling in opposite directions depending on which protein binds it.
